title: How much can language models memorize?
claim: Models memorize in proportion to data until capacity fills, then unintended memorization falls as training data grows past that point.
layout: 1 log-log line plot, three model-size curves, dashed dataset-size bound
description: A single log-log line chart on a cream background with grid lines. The x-axis is training set size, from 10^2 to 10^6 datapoints. The y-axis is unintended memorization in bits, from about 10^2 to 10^8. Three curves mark model sizes with hexagon markers: 3.6M in dark purple, 8.0M in blue, and 19.2M in yellow. A gray dashed diagonal line labeled 'Dataset size' (Total Bits in the legend) shows the upper bound. All three curves first overlap and rise along this line. Each then peaks and drops, with smaller models peaking earlier (about 10^4 for the purple curve) and larger ones later (about 10^5 for the yellow curve). A boxed legend sits at the lower left. The eye goes first to the rise-then-fall curves.
caption: Unintendedmemorizationoftext across model and dataset sizes (Section 4). All quantities are calculated with respect to a large oracle model trained on the full data distribution.
abstract: We propose a new method for estimating how much a model knows about a datapoint and use it to measure the capacity of modern language models. Prior studies of language model memorization have struggled to disentangle memorization from generalization. We formally separate memorization into two components: unintended memorization, the information a model contains about a specific dataset, and generalization, the information a model contains about the true data-generation process. When we completely eliminate generalization, we can compute the total memorization, which provides an estimate of model capacity: our measurements estimate that GPT-style models have a capacity of approximately 3.6 bits per parameter. We train language models on datasets of increasing size and observe that models memorize until their capacity fills, at which point "grokking" begins, and unintended memorization decreases as models begin to generalize. We train hundreds of transformer language models ranging from $500K$ to $1.5B$ parameters and produce a series of scaling laws relating model capacity and data size to membership inference.
